title: Lena and the Well
premise: When Jonah Whitlock returns to Hollow Creek to bury their twin brother Elias—killed by a fall into the old well on grandma's property—they find the house already occupied by a family that isn't there: a woman in 1970s clothing, two children, and an extra chair that appears in every photograph taken on the land. The chair belonged to Ada Merrick, a farmhand's daughter who vanished in 1974 after Jonah's grandmother stole the deed to her family's acreage, and her ghost has been waiting fifty years for someone to give it back. As the haunting tightens—Elias's voice beginning to answer from the well—Jonah, a forensic accountant and committed skeptic, must choose between protecting the inheritance that kept their fractured family afloat and restoring justice to the Merricks. In the end, Jonah burns the fraudulent deed, names Ada's descendants in a public reckoning, and lowers Elias's ashes into the well—not as a sacrifice, but as an apology—freeing both the dead and finally allowing themselves to grieve the twin they loved.
about_author: Ulyana Kavanagh is the pen name of a former rural land surveyor who spent a decade mapping disputed properties across Appalachia and collecting the stories that came with them. They write quiet, domestic horror about the debts families inherit along with their houses.

chapters.title: The Wrong Twin
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, first person. They arrive in Hollow Creek to arrange Elias's funeral, numb with grief and irritation at their grandmother's decaying house. The emotional beat is dissociation—Jonah treats death as paperwork. A neighbor mentions the well was capped in 1974 and un-capped last spring, planting the first wrongness.

chapters.title: One Chair Too Many
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Sorting Elias's belongings, Jonah finds photographs of the house spanning decades, each showing a plain wooden chair on the porch that appears in none of their memories. A Polaroid from the funeral shows the chair moved closer to the door. The beat is creeping dread beneath Jonah's rational explanations—lighting, lens flare, a prop left by a previous owner.

chapters.title: What Grandma Kept
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. In the attic they find a locked cedar chest: a 1974 property deed with a forged signature, a missing-persons clipping for Ada Merrick, and a child's shoe. Jonah's skepticism cracks for the first time. The emotional beat is the horror of discovering your beloved grandmother was a thief, and that the house itself is stolen goods.

chapters.title: The Woman at the Sink
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, interrupted once by a brief passage from Ada's 1974 diary. At 3 a.m. Jonah finds a woman in period clothing washing dishes that are already clean, humming a lullaby Jonah somehow knows. She says, 'You have his hands. He had hers.' The beat is terror fused with an awful, unwanted tenderness—the ghost treats Jonah like family.

chapters.title: Merrick Land
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. They track down Ruthie Merrick, Ada's granddaughter, now in her sixties, who confirms the family legend: grandma Whitlock forged the deed, Ada confronted her at the well, and Ada never came home. Ruthie wants nothing to do with the house. The beat is Jonah confronting justice outside any statute of limitations—and their first real ally.

chapters.title: Elias Answers
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, fraying. Grief breaks protocol: Jonah speaks into the well at night, and something with Elias's voice answers, asking to be let in. Jonah nearly opens the cap. The beat is the seduction of grief—horror wearing the face of the person Jonah misses most—and the realization that the haunting is offering a trade: the deed for the twin.

chapters.title: The Ledger
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Using forensic accounting skills, Jonah reconstructs fifty years of the fraud: rents collected, timber sold, interest compounded. They draft a restitution plan for the Merricks and confront the executor of grandma's estate, who threatens litigation. The beat is resolve—Jonah choosing justice over duty to the family name, knowing it will cost everything.

chapters.title: Nineteen Seventy-Four
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Ada's diary entries interleaved with Jonah reading them aloud in the house as the past bleeds into the present—the kitchen becomes 1974 around them. Ada's final entry describes the confrontation at the well. The beat is witness: the haunting was never malice, only an unanswered testimony, and Jonah is its first listener.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Climax at the well. The executor arrives with a court order; Elias's voice screams from below; the chair sits at the well's edge, waiting. Jonah publicly reads the fraud into a phone camera, hands Ruthie the original deed and the restitution ledger, and refuses the trade—telling Elias's voice, 'I love you, and I'm not bringing you back this way.' The beat is love against duty, chosen at last.

chapters.title: The Empty Chair
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, months later. The house is sold at a loss to a land trust; the Merricks' name is restored on the county records; Jonah scatters nothing and keeps everything—Elias's flannel, Ada's shoe returned to Ruthie. The final photograph of the porch shows no chair at all. The beat is grief finally allowed to be ordinary: not a haunting, just missing someone.
